subtitle: Relative clauses at full stretch, and holding a text together
words.intro: A *Stammtisch* is the table in the pub where the same people have sat for forty years, under a sign. All questions are settled here, the same way each Thursday, and nothing ever follows.

grammar[0].fact: A sentence can be perfectly correct and still impossible: Kafka, Mann and Kleist have sentences you can walk around in. German writing teachers today recommend no more than two levels of clause. Dr. Brummer’s generation didn’t get that memo.

grammar[1].fact: In a German essay you must not use the same noun twice in a row. So you’ll say *der Plan*, then *ein solcher Schritt*, then *diese Maßnahme*, and, at last, *das Vorhaben*. The reader’s job is to keep up. All of them mean the same plan.

document.intro: A real beer list from a taproom in Tübingen. The English has moved in: *Craft Bier*, *Tasting Tray*, *Pale Ale*. At the bottom, under *Klassisch*, are the two beers that the regulars at table four would order.
document.fact: The two columns are 0,3 and 0,5 litres, and every German menu has to say exactly how much you get. Your glass has a line on it, too. In a pub, people will sometimes point that line out, if the beer is under it.

reading.intro: Thursday, table four. Opa Heinz’s old friends have a problem. The pub’s new owner wants to take down the sign and move the table. Dr. Brummer, whose letters you’ll remember, has been asked to write a protest. He reads it out. It contains one sentence, and they are waiting for it to end.
reading.fact: The *Stammtisch* is a real institution, with a sign, *Stammtisch*, sitting in the middle of the table. It’s also a phrase: *Stammtischparolen* are the loud, simple claims that get made over the third beer. Politicians try to stay clear of the word and of the table.
